q: You are at anchor off Barbados and a crew member asks what the 13°05′N on the plotter actually measures. What do you tell them?
a: The arc of your meridian from the equator to here
o: The arc of the equator from Greenwich to here
The arc of your parallel from Greenwich to here
The arc of your meridian from the North Pole to here
why: Latitude is the arc of the meridian (the angle at the Earth's centre) from the equator: 13°05′ = 785 M north of it.

q: You are crossing the doldrums on a passage up the South Atlantic. How far is it along this track?
why: Contrary names add: 10°30′ + 4°15′ = 14°45′ of latitude × 60 = 885 M along a meridian.

q: You log your noon position in Horta, Azores. What does the 28°38′W measure?
a: The arc of the equator from Greenwich's meridian west to yours
o: The arc of the equator from Greenwich's meridian east to yours
The arc of the equator from the date line east to yours
The arc of your meridian from the equator north to Horta
why: Longitude is the arc of the equator (or the angle at the pole) between the Greenwich meridian and yours, 0–180° E or W.

q: You plan the passage from Fiji to Samoa across the 180th meridian. What is the difference of longitude, and which way?
You sketch the celestial sphere for your position at 30°N to show the crew where the sky's axis points. Which point is the north celestial pole?
a: B — 30° above the north point of the horizon
o: C — 60° above the north point of the horizon
D — 60° above the south point of the horizon
why: The altitude of the elevated pole equals your latitude: at 30°N the celestial pole stands 30° above due north.
ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

q: On a night watch in the South Atlantic you work out where the Sun is. Where is it on your celestial sphere?
a: At your nadir, 90° below the horizon
o: On your celestial horizon, due north
On the celestial equator, due north
why: The GP is your antipode, 180° of arc away, so the Sun is at the point directly below you: your nadir.

q: You are watching the Sun climb to noon on the passage from Bermuda to the Azores. Which circle of the celestial sphere is it crossing now?
a: Your meridian — the great circle through the poles and your zenith
o: Your celestial horizon — the circle 90° from your zenith
The celestial equator — the circle 90° from the poles
The ecliptic — the Sun's yearly path among the stars
why: The observer's meridian runs through both celestial poles, your zenith and nadir; the Sun bears 180° or 000° as it crosses it.

fig.title: Local noon, Bermuda to the Azores

q: You take a star sight from the cockpit. Why can't you put Hs straight into the PZX triangle?
a: It needs the altitude above the celestial horizon, through the Earth's centre
o: It needs the altitude above the visible horizon, at sea level
It needs the zenith distance, which a sextant cannot measure
It needs the altitude above the horizon at the body's GP
why: Hs is from the visible horizon at your eye; dip, refraction, SD and parallax reduce it to Ho above the celestial horizon.
ref: Celestial sphere — celestial and visible horizon

fig.title: Sight at dusk
lines: Hs read against the visible horizon

q: You want to know over which ocean the Sun stands at this moment. Where is its geographical position (GP)?
why: GP latitude = Dec; GP longitude = GHA west up to 180°, else 360° − GHA east: 360° − 210°46.1′ = 149°13.9′E.

q: You read the Sun's data for the moment of your sight. What is the position of its GP?
why: Dec is the GP's latitude and GHA (under 180°) its west longitude: 7°33.3′S 48°23.4′W.

q: You take a morning sight of the Sun off Bermuda. What LHA do you use?
You are approaching the Maldives and take a morning sun sight. What LHA do you use?
On the SSB net you compare sun sights with a yacht 300 miles from you on the ARC. How can both altitudes be the same?
a: Both yachts lie on one circle of equal altitude round the GP
o: Both yachts lie on the same meridian as the GP
Both yachts lie on the same parallel as the GP
Both yachts lie on the great circle through the GP
why: Everyone the same distance from the GP sees the same altitude: a circle of radius 90° − 52°10′ = 37°50′ = 2270 M.

fig.title: SSB net, 1423 UT
lines: Both sights at the same second

q: You reduce this sun sight in mid-Atlantic. What is the radius of the circle of position it puts you on?
why: Zenith distance 90° − 61°20.0′ = 28°40.0′ = 1720′ of arc, and 1′ of arc = 1 M.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

q: You reduce a sun sight with Ho 41°15′ and draw the position line as a straight line on your plotting sheet. Why is that good enough?
a: The circle's radius is 2925 M; near the AP its arc is almost straight
o: The circle is a meridian, so it is straight on the chart
On a Mercator sheet every great circle plots straight
The intercept corrects for the curve, so it does not matter
why: The circle of equal altitude is huge; the few miles of it near the AP plot as a straight line at right angles to the azimuth.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

q: You plot this sun sight on the plotting sheet. Which way does the position line run?
a: 045°–225°, at right angles to the azimuth
why: A position line is a short piece of the circle of equal altitude, at right angles to the bearing of the GP.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

q: You take a dawn sight of Arcturus. How far are you from the star's geographical position?
why: Distance from the GP = zenith distance: 90° − 35°45.0′ = 54°15.0′ = 3255′ = 3255 M.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

q: In the Caribbean in June the Sun near noon is almost overhead. How do you use this sight?
a: Draw a circle of 90 M radius round the Sun's GP
o: Reduce it from an AP and draw a straight line
Discard it, since no sight above 80° can be used
Take it as a meridian altitude for latitude only
why: Zenith distance 90° − 88°30′ = 1°30′ = 90 M: too curved for a straight line, so plot the circle itself round the GP.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — high-altitude sights

fig.title: Sun near noon, the Caribbean, June
lines: Sun's GP from the almanac, to the second

q: You sketch the PZX triangle for a star sight. Which side gives you the star's altitude?
o: PX — the altitude is PX − PZ
why: ZX is the zenith distance, your distance from the star's GP, so the altitude is 90° − ZX.

fig.note: Your PZX triangle on the celestial sphere

q: You set up the PZX triangle for Arcturus south of the Cape of Good Hope. What are the sides PZ and PX?
why: In the south P is the South Pole: PZ = 90° − 35° = 55°; a north Dec lies beyond the equator, so PX = 90° + 19°06′.

q: You set up the PZX triangle for Vega off Bermuda. What is the polar distance PX?
why: Dec has the same name as the elevated pole: PX = 90° − Dec = 90° − 38°48′ = 51°12′.

q: You set up the PZX triangle for this star. What is the angle at P, and on which side?
why: LHA over 180° means the body is east: the angle at P (meridian angle) = 360° − 300° = 60°E.
ref: PZX triangle — the angle at P

q: You solve the PZX triangle for a sight. Which three parts do you already know?
a: PZ from your AP, PX from the Dec, and the angle at P from the LHA
o: PZ from your AP, ZX from the Ho, and the angle at Z from the compass
PX from the Dec, ZX from the Ho, and the angle at X from the SHA
PZ from the Ho, PX from the GHA, and the angle at P from the UT
why: Co-lat, polar distance and LHA give ZX (so Hc = 90° − ZX) and the angle at Z, the azimuth.

q: You solve the PZX triangle by the cosine formula. What calculated altitude Hc do you get?
You work an afternoon sun sight north of the equator. What is the true azimuth Zn?
why: Z is measured from the north (elevated) pole towards the west: Zn = 360° − 100° = 260°.

q: You work a morning sun sight off South Africa at 33°S. What is the true azimuth Zn?
why: South of the equator Z is measured from the south pole: S86°E gives Zn = 180° − 86° = 094°.

q: You notice the almanac gives Aries a GHA for every hour but each star only an SHA. Why does that work?
a: The stars keep their places relative to Aries; the sky turns as one
o: The stars move 15° an hour, the same as the Sun
Each star's SHA grows 15° an hour, like a GHA
Aries is a bright star the others are measured from
why: SHA is measured westward from Aries and barely changes, so GHA★ = GHA Aries + SHA at any moment.

fig.title: Almanac, daily page
lines: Stars: SHA and Dec, once per page

q: You are reducing a dusk sight of Vega. What is the star's GHA?
You take Sirius at dawn on the way to the Cape Verdes. What is its GHA?
You want to catch Vega on your meridian again tomorrow night at the same longitude. When will it come?
why: Aries gains 2.46′ an hour on the Sun: the stars come round in 23 h 56 min, so about 4 min earlier each night.
ref: First point of Aries — the sidereal day

q: You take two sun sights on the same day. Between them, how far has the Sun's GP moved?
why: The Earth turns 360° in 24 h, so the Sun's GHA grows 15° an hour: 4 h × 15° = 60° west.

q: You explain to the crew how fast the Sun's GP races across the ocean today. About how fast is it?
why: 15° an hour = 900′ of longitude; along the parallel of 23°26.3′N that is 900 × cos 23°26.3′ ≈ 826 M an hour.

q: You turn to the Sun's column for the longest day in the north. About what Dec do you expect?
why: The ecliptic is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator; at the June solstice the Sun reaches its greatest north Dec.
ref: Declination through the year — the ecliptic

q: You prepare for the noon sight on the first day of the ARC. About what Dec will the almanac give?
why: The Dec changes fast near the equinox and slowly near the solstice: on 23 Nov it is already S20°24′.

q: By mistake you work your noon sight with yesterday's Dec. In which month does that cost you the most?
a: March — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
o: June — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
December — the Dec changes about 24′ a day
Any month — the Dec changes 24′ every day
why: Near the equinoxes the Sun crosses the equator at about 24′ a day; near the solstices its Dec barely moves.

q: You are at 50°N, setting out from the Channel for the Azores. Which of these stars never sets for you?
why: A body is circumpolar when Dec > co-lat (90° − 50° = 40°): only Capella (46°01′) qualifies; Vega (38°48′) just sets.

q: You are south of the Cape at 35°S. Which of these stars stays above your horizon all night, every night?
why: Co-lat 90° − 35° = 55°: Acrux (S63°14′) is circumpolar; Canopus (S52°43′) dips below the south horizon.

q: You are waiting for the noon sight off Martinique. What altitude and bearing do you expect at meridian passage?
why: The Dec is north of your latitude: z = 23°26.3′ − 14°36′ = 8°50.3′; highest altitude 81°09.7′, Sun to the north.

q: You plan a meridian sight of Sirius before leaving Las Palmas. What will its altitude be?
why: Contrary names: z = 28°08′ + 16°45′ = 44°53′, so the highest altitude is 45°07′, due south.

q: On the passage from Horta to Mindelo, how much lower will the celestial pole stand when you arrive?
why: The altitude of the celestial pole equals your latitude: 38°32′ − 16°53′ = 21°39′ lower.
ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

q: You are crossing the South Atlantic at 40°S on the equinox. Where will the Sun rise?
why: With Dec 0° the Sun is on the celestial equator, which meets every horizon due east and due west.

q: You are on passage to Mauritius at 20°S. Can you use Vega for a star sight?
a: Yes — it rises to 31°12′ over the north horizon
o: No — a northern star never rises south of the equator
Yes — it is circumpolar at your latitude
Yes — it rises to 58°48′ over the north horizon
why: Vega rises because its Dec (38°48′) is less than your co-lat (70°); z = 20° + 38°48′ = 58°48′, so at best 31°12′ high.

q: A crew member wants to see the Southern Cross from the Azores. What do you tell them?
a: It never rises — its Dec is more than your co-lat 52°16′
o: It never sets — its Dec is more than your co-lat 52°16′
It rises 10°58′ above the south horizon at its highest
It rises only in summer, low over the south horizon
why: Contrary name and Dec 63°14′ > co-lat 52°16′: even at meridian passage Acrux stays 10°58′ below your horizon.

fig.title: Ponta Delgada, 37°44′N
lines: Brightest star of the Southern Cross

q: You explain to the crew why the noon sight needs no LHA, no AP and no tables. What is the reason?
a: P, Z and X lie on your meridian, so the triangle collapses into one arc
o: At noon the Sun's GP is always on the equator below you
At noon the azimuth is 000° or 180°, so Hc equals Ho
At noon the Sun stops moving, so the time does not matter
why: On the meridian PZ, PX and ZX lie along one arc: latitude = Dec ± zenith distance, with no LHA needed.
ref: Meridian altitude — why it gives latitude

q: You take the noon sight on your way to Tahiti. What is your latitude?
why: z = 90° − 80°59.0′ = 9°01.0′; the Sun bears north, so you are z south of its GP: 7°19.0′ + 9°01.0′ = 16°20.0′S.
ref: Meridian altitude — why it gives latitude

q: Before a dusk star fix south of Madagascar you want the GP of Canopus. Where is it?
You take Arcturus at dawn off Tahiti. What is its LHA, and where is the star?
You watch Capella through a long winter night at 50°N. What are its highest and lowest altitudes?
why: Upper: 90° − (50° − 46°01′) = 86°01′ to the south. Lower: lat − polar distance = 50° − 43°59′ = 6°01′ to the north.
ref: Circumpolar bodies — upper and lower transit

q: You solve the PZX triangle for Regulus in the South Atlantic. What is Hc?
You consider Canopus for a meridian sight before leaving Las Palmas. Is it a good choice?
a: No — at best 9°09′ high, where refraction is large
o: No — it never rises at Las Palmas
Yes — at its highest it stands 65°25′ due south
Yes — it is circumpolar and can be taken all night
why: z = 28°08′ + 52°43′ = 80°51′: Canopus culminates only 9°09′ above the south horizon; avoid sights below about 10°.

q: You notice that the Sun's GHA on the almanac's daily page grows by almost exactly 15° every hour. Why 15°?
a: The Earth turns once against the Sun in 24 hours
o: The Earth moves 15° along its orbit every hour
The Sun moves 15° east among the stars every hour
The Earth turns once against the stars in 24 hours
why: One turn against the Sun, 360°, takes 24 h of mean time: 360° ÷ 24 = 15° an hour; against the stars it takes 4 min less.

q: You cross the equator on the way to Brazil and a crew member asks where the celestial poles are now. What do you tell them?
a: On your horizon, due north and due south
o: One at your zenith, the other at your nadir
Both 23°26′ above your horizon, north and south
The north one 90° up, the south one 90° down
why: The elevated pole's altitude equals your latitude: at 0° both celestial poles sit on the horizon, at the north and south points.
ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

q: At sunrise, with the Sun's centre on your celestial horizon, a crew member asks how far away its GP is. What is the answer?
why: Zenith distance 90° − 0° = 90° = 5400′ of arc = 5400 M: a quarter of the way round the Earth from the GP.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

fig.title: Sunrise, Indian Ocean
lines: Sun's centre on the celestial horizon

q: At anchor off Cape Town, a crew member asks where the sky's south pole is. What do you tell them?
a: 33°55′ above the south point of the horizon
o: 56°05′ above the south point of the horizon
33°55′ above the north point of the horizon
why: The elevated pole's altitude equals your latitude; south of the equator it is the south celestial pole, 33°55′ up, due south.
ref: Celestial sphere — altitude of the pole

fig.title: Table Bay, at anchor
lines: Clear night, no star at the pole

q: You label the parts of your PZX triangle for a star sight south of the equator. Which part does the sight reduction never use?
a: The angle at X, at the star
o: The angle at P, at the pole
The angle at Z, at your zenith
The side PX, the polar distance
why: Reduction takes PZ, PX and the angle at P (LHA) and finds ZX (Hc) and the angle at Z (azimuth); the angle at X is not needed.

q: Becalmed on the equator, a crew member asks which stars stay above the horizon all night. What do you tell them?
a: None — every star rises and sets
o: Acrux and the stars near the south pole
Capella and the stars near the north pole
The stars within 23°26′ of the equator
why: Circumpolar needs Dec > co-lat; on the equator the co-lat is 90°, so every star spends half its daily circle below the horizon.

q: On passage to Australia you work out the Sun's LHA for your sight. Where is the Sun?
a: West of your meridian — it is afternoon
o: East of your meridian — it is morning
On your meridian — it is noon
Below your horizon — it is night
why: LHA is counted westward from your meridian: 0°–180° puts the body west of you (afternoon), over 180° east (morning).

q: A crew member says it is summer in the south in January because the Earth is then closest to the Sun. What do you tell them?
a: No — it is the axis's 23°26′ tilt to the ecliptic
o: Yes — the Earth is about 3% closer to the Sun then
No — the Sun's Dec is 23°26′ north in January
Yes — the southern oceans are nearer the Sun then
why: The equator is tilted 23°26′ to the ecliptic, so the Sun's Dec swings N and S; in January its GP is far south — and the north has winter.

q: You want to catch Arcturus as it rises. Where on the horizon do you look?
why: A body rises on the side of east named like its Dec: a north Dec rises north of east, whichever hemisphere you are in.

fig.title: Star watch off Durban
lines: Due to rise within the hour

q: On the SSB net five yachts spread across the ocean compare sun sights taken at the same second. Which pair of values is the same for all of them?
why: GHA and Dec fix the GP, the same for everyone at one instant; LHA, Hc and Zn depend on each yacht's own position.

fig.title: SSB net, 1200 UT
lines: All take a sun sight at 1200 UT

q: You take a sun sight off Fiji, close to the 180th meridian. What LHA do you use, and where is the Sun?
On the passage from Vanuatu to Fiji you picture where the Sun stands. How far is its GP from your meridian, and which way?
o: 6°22.9′ east, this side of the 180th meridian

q: On New Year's Day you explain the date line to the crew. At that moment, what is the local time and date at the GP, just either side of the line?
a: Noon, 1 Jan to the west of the line; noon, 31 Dec to the east
o: Noon, 31 Dec to the west of the line; noon, 1 Jan to the east
Midnight, 1 Jan to the west of the line; midnight, 31 Dec to the east
Noon, 1 Jan to the west of the line; noon, 2 Jan to the east
why: Under the GP it is local noon; west of 180° the date is a day ahead of the east side: 1 January to the west, 31 December to the east.

q: Waiting in Tonga for a weather window to New Zealand, a crew member asks on which days the noon Sun stands straight overhead here. What do you tell them?
o: Never — only on the Tropic of Capricorn
why: The Sun is overhead at noon when its Dec equals your latitude, S21°08′: passed going south in late Nov and coming back in mid-Jan.
ref: The Sun's declination through the year

fig.title: Nuku'alofa, Tonga
lines: Sun Dec 20 Nov S19°38′ · 30 Nov S21°36′

q: Off Rio on the solstice, the crew expects the noon Sun to the north, as usual in the southern hemisphere. Which way do you face for the noon sight, and how high is the Sun?
why: Dec S23°26.3′ is south of 22°54′S: the GP is 0°32.3′ south of you, so the Sun bears south, 90° − 0°32.3′ = 89°27.7′ high.

q: Before leaving Cape Town for St Helena you take a noon sight. Which way does the Sun bear, and how high is it?
why: The GP (S21°57.3′) is 11°57.7′ north of you: even in the southern summer the Sun bears north, 90° − 11°57.7′ = 78°02.3′.

fig.title: Noon, 10 Jan, Table Bay
lines: The height of the southern summer

q: You take a noon sight in the Galápagos on the equinox. Which way does the Sun bear, and how high is it?
why: Contrary names: z = 0°45.0′ + 0°03.5′ = 0°48.5′, GP north of you: the Sun bears north, 90° − 0°48.5′ = 89°11.5′ high.

q: At anchor in Bora Bora you watch the noon Sun pass straight overhead. Which way does it bear a few minutes before and a few minutes after noon?
a: Nearly east before noon, nearly west after
o: Nearly north before noon, nearly south after
Due north both before and after noon
Nearly south before noon, nearly north after
why: Its GP runs west along your own parallel and passes over you: the azimuth swings from about 090° to about 270°, never N or S.

q: In the Bahamas on the longest day, a crew member says the noon Sun will stand to the north of you. Is that right?
a: No — the Sun's GP never goes north of 23°26′N
o: Yes — around the June solstice, at noon
Yes — whenever the Sun's Dec is north
No — north of the equator it never does
why: The Sun's GP never leaves the tropics: at 25°03′N it is always south of you at noon, at best 88°23′ high on 21 June.
ref: The Sun's declination through the year

q: Running east in the forties, you plan a meridian sight of Antares. Which way will it bear, and how high will it be?
why: Dec S26°29′ lies north of 40°S: z = 40° − 26°29′ = 13°31′, so Antares culminates to the north, 76°29′ high.

q: Waiting in Horta, a crew member wants to see a body pass straight overhead. Which of these comes closest to your zenith?
o: The Sun at the June solstice
why: At culmination z = |lat − Dec|: Vega 16′, Capella 7°29′, the Sun at best 15°06′, Arcturus 19°26′ from your zenith.

q: A crew member asks why the Sun is highest exactly as it crosses your meridian. What do you tell them?
a: Its GP then passes closest to you on its way west
o: Refraction is least when the Sun bears N or S
The Sun's Dec peaks at the moment of local noon
The Earth turns most slowly at local noon
why: The GP runs west along the parallel of its Dec and is nearest you as it crosses your meridian: ZX least, altitude greatest.

q: Southbound from the Cape Verdes, a crew member wants Acrux to stay up all night. From which latitude will it never set?
why: Circumpolar when Dec > co-lat: 63°14′ > 90° − lat once you are south of 90° − 63°14′ = 26°46′S.

fig.title: Cape Verdes to Cape Town
lines: Brightest star of the Southern Cross

q: On a charter south from Ushuaia, a guest asks from which latitude the Sun stays above the horizon all day at the solstice. What do you answer (ignore refraction)?
why: The Sun is circumpolar when its Dec exceeds your co-lat: 23°26′ > 90° − lat south of 66°34′S, the Antarctic Circle.

q: You plan the watches for a solstice departure from Cape Town. Where does the Sun rise, and is it up for more or less than 12 hours?
a: South of east; more than 12 hours
o: North of east; more than 12 hours
South of east; less than 12 hours
why: Dec of the same name as your latitude: the Sun rises south of east, and more than half its daily circle is above your horizon.

q: Ten degrees south of the line you set up the first PZX triangle of the passage. Which pole is P, and how high does it stand?
a: The south celestial pole, 10° above the south horizon
o: The north celestial pole, 10° below the north horizon
The south celestial pole, 80° above the south horizon
The north celestial pole, right on the north horizon
why: P is the elevated pole, named like your latitude: at 10°S the south celestial pole stands 10° up, and PZ = 80°.

q: You set up the PZX triangle for a morning sun sight off Durban. What are the sides PZ and PX?
why: P is the south pole: PZ = 90° − 29°53.0′ = 60°07.0′; a south Dec is on your side, so PX = 90° − 17°08.6′ = 72°51.4′.

q: Bound for Brisbane, you have the azimuth angle from your afternoon sun reduction. Which true azimuth do you lay off on the plotting sheet?
why: South of the equator Z is measured from south: S82°W is 180° + 82° = 262°, the Sun just south of west.

q: While the GPS still works you check your sextant work against it. What Ho should the sight give?
why: 1500 M = 1500′ of arc = 25°00′ of zenith distance, so Ho = 90° − 25°00′ = 65°00′.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — zenith distance

fig.title: Sextant practice, GPS on
lines: GPS: 1500 M from the Sun's GP
At the second of the sight

q: You draw two simultaneous star sights as whole circles of equal altitude. They cross at A and at B, about 2900 M apart. Where are you?
a: At A, the crossing near your DR
o: At A or B — only a third star can tell
why: Two circles always cross twice, usually thousands of miles apart; your DR (or a third body) shows which crossing is yours.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

fig.note: Two star sights at one instant · not to scale

q: You and the mate reduce the same sun sight from different assumed positions and get different intercepts. What do you find when you plot both?
a: Both give the same position line
o: The two lines lie 30 M apart
The two lines cross at your position
Only the AP nearer the GP gives the line
why: AP 1 + 12 M south = AP 2 + 18 M north: one line. It is a piece of one circle round the GP; the AP only changes the intercept.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — the assumed position

fig.title: One sun sight, two navigators
lines: Mate: AP 2, 30 M south of AP 1

q: You discover that the index error was left out of your morning sun sight. Where does the position line you plotted lie compared with the true one?
why: On the arc, so Ho came out 2.0′ too high: the zenith distance and the circle's radius are 2 M short, so the line sits 2 M nearer the Sun.

fig.title: Morning sun line
lines: Index error found later: 2.0′ on the arc
It was not applied to this sight

q: You discover that the watch used for yesterday's sights was 30 seconds fast. What has that done to yesterday's fixes?
a: Moved them 7.5′ of longitude west; latitude unchanged
o: Moved them 7.5′ of longitude east; latitude unchanged
Moved them 7.5′ of latitude south; longitude unchanged
Moved them 0.5′ of longitude west; latitude unchanged
why: UT 30 s late makes every GHA 7.5′ too big and every GP too far west: the whole picture is turned 7.5′ west about the pole.

fig.title: Watch check by GPS time
lines: Used for all of yesterday's sights

q: Halfway across on the ARC you take a sun sight just as the Sun bears due east. Which way does the position line run, and what does it give you?
why: A position line lies at right angles to the azimuth: with the Sun due east it runs along your meridian and fixes longitude.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — position line

q: You want to mark Jupiter on your star finder, which places bodies by their SHA. What SHA do you use?
why: SHA is measured west from Aries: SHA = GHA body − GHA Aries = 120°10.4′ − 95°40.2′ = 24°30.2′.
ref: First point of Aries and SHA

fig.title: Almanac, 1900 UT
lines: Star finder: bodies set by SHA

q: At dusk you want a star that is crossing your meridian right now. Which one is it?
why: On your meridian LHA★ = LHA Aries + SHA = 360°: SHA = 360° − 279°27′ = 80°33′, which is Vega.
ref: First point of Aries and SHA

q: On a long night watch you picture the GP of Sirius moving across the globe. Which way does it go?
a: West along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°02.5′ an hour
o: East along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°02.5′ an hour
West along a great circle, 15°02.5′ an hour
West along the 16°45′S parallel, 15°00.0′ an hour
why: A star's Dec is fixed, so its GP keeps to the parallel of its Dec; its GHA (Aries + SHA) grows 15°02.5′ an hour, westward.

q: Before a dawn star fix on the way from Tonga to Fiji you want the GP of Antares. Where is it?
Leafing through a year of almanac pages, the crew notice that the Sun's Dec swings while Vega's stays put. Why?
a: The Sun goes round the ecliptic, tilted 23°26′ to the equator
o: The Sun is close, so its parallax shifts its Dec
The Earth's axis nods 23°26′ to and fro each year
The Sun moves along the celestial equator, the stars do not
why: As the Earth orbits, the Sun seems to circle the ecliptic once a year, and that circle is tilted 23°26′ to the celestial equator.

q: You plan Moon sights for the week ahead. Why does the Moon cross your meridian about 50 minutes later each night?
a: It moves east among the stars about 13° a day
o: It moves west among the stars about 13° a day
Its Dec changes by about 13° a day
Its GHA grows faster than the Sun's
why: The Moon orbits eastward about 13° a day against the stars, so its GHA grows only about 14°30′ an hour and it comes round later.

q: You plotted a high sun sight as a straight line and crossed it with a star line 60 M from the foot of the intercept, F. How far is that fix from the true circle of position?
why: Offset ≈ d² ÷ 2r = 60² ÷ (2 × 240) ≈ 7.4 M: near the zenith the circle is tight, so plot the circle itself or keep the AP close.
ref: Circle of equal altitude — high-altitude sights

q: You find you reduced this morning's sun sight with yesterday's Dec. How far is the position line out, and which way?
why: The GP sits 23.7 M too far south; along Zn 120° that is 23.7 × cos 60° ≈ 12 M, so the line lies 12 M too far towards 120°.

q: You reduce a morning sun sight off the Cape in the southern summer. What are Hc and Zn?
why: Lat −34°, Dec −19°00.0′: sin Hc = sin 34° sin 19°00.0′ + cos 34° cos 19°00.0′ cos 315° → 47°25.2′; Sun north of east, Zn 081°.

fig.title: Morning sun, 25 Jan, off the Cape

q: You plan star sights for a long passage along 35°S. For how long is Arcturus above your horizon each day?
why: Rising LHA: cos LHA = −tan lat tan Dec = tan 35° tan 19°06′ (lat S) → 76°; up for 152° of its circle ≈ 10 h.

q: Running east at 45°S, you watch Acrux circle the pole through the night. What are its highest and lowest altitudes?
o: 71°46′ to the south and 18°14′ to the north
71°46′ to the north and 18°14′ to the south
why: Upper: 90° − (63°14′ − 45°) = 71°46′, GP south of you. Lower: lat − polar distance = 45° − 26°46′ = 18°14′, below the pole.
ref: Circumpolar bodies — upper and lower transit

q: Off Mauritius at dusk you are reducing a sight of Antares. Which LHA goes into the triangle, and on which side of your meridian is the star?
On the solstice at 30°S the Sun rises south of east and swings round to the north by noon. At what altitude does it bear due east (090°)?
why: Bearing 090° the triangle has a right angle at Z: sin Hc = sin Dec ÷ sin lat = sin 23°26.2′ ÷ sin 30° → 52°42′.

q: You and a buddy boat, either side of the 180th meridian, take sun sights at the same second. What LHA does each of you use?
why: You: 170° + 178°E = 348°. Buddy: 170° − 178°W = −8° + 360° = 352°. They are 4° east of you, so their LHA is 4° more.

q: You reduce a morning sun sight in the southern summer and get an absurd intercept. Which slip is the most likely cause?
a: The Dec named north instead of south
o: The index error applied the wrong way
The dip added instead of subtracted
Yesterday's Dec used instead of today's
why: IE, dip or a day's Dec cost minutes at most; a Dec of the wrong name moves the GP by twice the Dec, here about 45°.

q: South of the Cape of Good Hope you reduce a dawn sight of Arcturus. What are Hc and Zn?
why: Lat −35°, Dec +19°06′: sin Hc = −sin 35° sin 19°06′ + cos 35° cos 19°06′ cos 330° → 28°51.6′; star NE of you, Zn 033°.
